question: According to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1569 as regards qualified electronic attestations of attributes (QEAAs) and electronic attestations of attributes provided by or on behalf of a public sector body responsible for an authentic source (Pub-EAAs), the Commission was obliged to fulfil its obligations under Articles 6-9 of the Regulation by 19 August 2026. 1.
Which Member States were (a) on time; (b) late; or (c) not yet ready to establish a list of public sector bodies or develop the verification mechanism for qualified trust service providers?
Why has the Commission not published either the list of public sector bodies, or the catalogues of attributes and of schemes for the attestation of attributes to this date?

Please explain the current level of uptake and use of Pub-EAAs and QEAAs across the EU, referring to the number of issuers and attestations created, and the reasons for it, such as major challenges that continue to hinder their uptake.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.11.2026) Member States are required to provide European Digital Identity Wallets by the end of December 2026. As the Wallets are deployed, uptake and use of electronic attestations of attributes (EAAs) are expected to grow rapidly.

By 24 December 2026, Member States shall ensure that the attributes listed in Annex VI to Regulation (EU) No 910/2014, including address, age, gender, civil status, etc., are made available for verification by qualified trust service providers issuing electronic attestations of attributes. There is no deadline for Member States to establish a list of public sector bodies.

The provision of electronic attestation of attributes issued by or on behalf of a public sector body responsible for an authentic source (Pub-EAAs) and qualified electronic attestations of attributes (QEAAs) is possible under the applicable conditions but is not mandatory. Member States have not yet notified any providers of Pub-EAAs.

The Commission is technically ready to receive such notifications and publish the corresponding information once received. To date, three qualified trust service providers have been notified as qualified to issue QEAAs. The Commission does not collect data on the number of attestations issued by these providers. Consequently, the actual volume of issuance and level of uptake cannot be assessed.
Further information is available on the eIDAS Dashboard1, including the dedicated section on Pub-EAA providers.
